topic.en: Three texts: how scientists learned to detect gravitational waves, how heat pumps warm homes, and the argument about self-driving cars.
topic.kk: Үш мәтін: адамдар гравитациялық толқындарды қалай «естіді», жылу сорғысы үйді қалай жылытады және жүргізушісіз көліктер туралы талқы.
topic.ru: Три текста: как люди научились «слышать» гравитационные волны, как тепловой насос греет дом, и спор о беспилотных автомобилях.

paragraphs.text: For almost all of history, astronomy has depended on light. Everything known about the stars and galaxies, from their distances to their chemical composition, was learned by collecting the light they emit or the radio waves, X-rays and other forms of radiation that belong to the same family. In 2015 that changed. For the first time, scientists detected ripples in space itself, produced by two black holes that had spiralled together and merged more than a billion years earlier, and a new way of observing the universe began. Light, however, cannot reveal everything, since some of the most violent events in the universe emit very little of it, and the discovery was announced only after months of careful checking.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The existence of such ripples had been predicted a century before. According to the theory of general relativity, massive objects distort the space around them, and when they accelerate, as two stars orbiting each other do, they send out waves of distortion that travel at the speed of light. These gravitational waves stretch and squeeze space as they pass, but the effect is extraordinarily small. Even the author of the theory doubted that they would ever be detected, since the changes they produce in distances on Earth are far smaller than the width of an atom. For decades, the only evidence for gravitational waves was indirect, coming from the slow shrinking of the orbits of certain pairs of stars.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Detecting them required instruments of astonishing sensitivity. The detectors that made the first observation consist of two long arms, each four kilometres in length, arranged in an L shape. A laser beam is split and sent along both arms, reflected by mirrors at the ends and recombined. When a gravitational wave passes, it lengthens one arm very slightly while shortening the other, altering the way the two beams combine. The change to be measured is less than a thousandth of the diameter of a proton, which meant that the instruments had to be isolated from vibrations caused by traffic, waves on distant coasts and even the movement of air. The laser light travels back and forth many times along each arm, effectively lengthening the detector, and the mirrors are suspended on fine fibres so that they hang almost perfectly still.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Because such tiny signals can easily be imitated by local disturbances, detectors are built in pairs thousands of kilometres apart. A genuine gravitational wave reaches both within a few thousandths of a second, while a passing lorry or a small earthquake affects only one. The difference in arrival times also helps astronomers work out where in the sky the wave came from, and adding more detectors in other countries has made those estimates considerably more precise. The two detectors of the first observatory are located on opposite sides of a single country.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The signals themselves carry a great deal of information. As two black holes spiral towards each other, the waves they emit rise in both frequency and strength, producing a pattern that researchers compare to the chirp of a bird. By matching the observed pattern with calculations, scientists can estimate the masses of the objects, how fast they were spinning and how far away they were. The first detection revealed black holes about thirty times as massive as the sun, larger than many astronomers had expected to find in pairs. The whole signal from the first detection lasted less than a second, and similar calculations can even be used to test whether general relativity holds under extreme conditions.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: In 2017 detectors recorded waves from the collision of two neutron stars, the extremely dense remains of exploded stars. Within two seconds, a satellite observed a burst of gamma rays from the same region, and over the following weeks telescopes around the world watched the glowing aftermath in visible light, infrared and X-rays. The observations showed that such collisions produce large quantities of heavy elements, including gold and platinum, and confirmed that gravitational waves travel at the same speed as light. The event was the first in which the same source was observed with both gravitational waves and light.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Since then, detections have become routine, with dozens of events recorded in each observing run. The growing catalogue is allowing astronomers to study how often black holes merge, how large they can become and how they form in the first place. Some of the objects detected fall in a range of masses that current theories struggle to explain, suggesting that some black holes may be the product of earlier mergers. Detections of neutron stars merging with black holes have also been reported.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Future instruments aim to detect waves that current detectors cannot. A planned observatory in space, consisting of three spacecraft millions of kilometres apart, would be sensitive to the slow waves produced by merging giant black holes at the centres of galaxies. Meanwhile, astronomers timing the regular pulses of distant spinning stars have found evidence of a faint background of gravitational waves, perhaps produced by countless pairs of such giant black holes across the universe. A century after it was predicted, gravitational wave astronomy is still at the beginning of what it may reveal. The scientists who led the construction of the first detectors were awarded a Nobel Prize in 2017.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: Heating buildings accounts for a large share of the energy used in cold and temperate countries, and most of that heat has traditionally come from burning gas, oil or coal. As governments try to reduce emissions, attention has turned to a technology that has existed for well over a century but has only recently become common in homes: the heat pump. Rather than generating heat by burning fuel, a heat pump moves heat that already exists from one place to another, usually from the air or the ground outside into a building. The idea is simple, but its widespread use has been slow to arrive; in some countries they are already the most common form of heating in new homes.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The principle is the same as that of a refrigerator, which removes heat from the food inside it and releases it through the coils at the back. A heat pump simply runs this process on a larger scale and in the opposite direction, taking heat from outdoors and releasing it indoors. That it can extract useful heat from cold outdoor air seems surprising, but even air at several degrees below freezing contains a considerable amount of heat energy, which can be captured if the working fluid inside the pump is colder still. Many heat pumps can also run in reverse, cooling a building in summer.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The cycle has four main stages. A liquid refrigerant with a very low boiling point passes through a heat exchanger outside, where it absorbs heat from the air or ground and evaporates into a gas. The gas is then compressed, which raises its temperature sharply. The hot gas passes through a second heat exchanger inside the building, where it releases its heat into water for radiators or into the air, and condenses back into a liquid. Finally, the liquid passes through an expansion valve, which lowers its pressure and temperature, and the cycle begins again. The refrigerants used have changed over time, as earlier chemicals were found to damage the ozone layer or to warm the climate if they leaked.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The great advantage of a heat pump is its efficiency. Because it moves heat rather than creating it, a heat pump typically delivers three to four units of heat for every unit of electricity it consumes, whereas even the best gas boiler delivers slightly less than one unit of heat per unit of fuel. This ratio, known as the coefficient of performance, depends on the difference between the outdoor temperature and the temperature required indoors: the colder it is outside, the harder the pump must work and the lower its efficiency becomes. Manufacturers usually quote an average efficiency over a whole heating season rather than a single figure, and even in cold weather a well-designed system rarely delivers less than two units of heat per unit of electricity.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: This relationship has important consequences for how heat pumps are used. They work best with heating systems that operate at relatively low temperatures, such as underfloor heating or large radiators, and in buildings that are well insulated, so that heat is not lost as quickly as it is supplied. In older, draughty houses heated by small radiators designed for very hot water from a boiler, a heat pump may struggle to keep rooms warm on the coldest days unless the building is improved first, which can add considerably to the cost of installation. Installers therefore often recommend improving insulation before, rather than after, a heat pump is fitted.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Ground-source heat pumps draw heat from pipes buried in the garden or from deep boreholes, taking advantage of the fact that the temperature a few metres underground remains fairly constant throughout the year. They are more efficient than air-source pumps in very cold weather, but installation is more expensive and requires land or drilling. Air-source pumps, which extract heat from outdoor air using a unit similar to that of an air conditioner, are cheaper and simpler to fit and have become by far the most common type in homes. Some cities are building networks that supply several buildings from a single large heat pump.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Early models acquired a poor reputation in some countries, partly because they were installed in unsuitable buildings or sized incorrectly, leaving occupants cold. Modern designs perform far better in freezing conditions, and some of the countries with the highest proportion of homes heated by heat pumps are among the coldest in Europe. There, the technology is regarded as ordinary, and installers are experienced in fitting systems to the needs of individual houses. Training enough installers has become a challenge in countries where demand has risen quickly.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Cost remains the main barrier. A heat pump is usually more expensive to buy and install than a boiler, and whether it is cheaper to run depends on the relative prices of electricity and gas, which vary greatly between countries. Many governments now offer grants to cover part of the installation cost. As electricity increasingly comes from wind and solar power, heating homes with heat pumps also reduces emissions further each year, an advantage that a boiler burning fossil fuel can never offer. Some electricity companies also offer cheaper prices at night, which heat pumps can take advantage of.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: For more than a decade, companies have promised that cars able to drive themselves are only a few years away. Test vehicles have covered millions of kilometres on public roads, and in a small number of cities it is now possible to hail a taxi with no driver. Yet the widespread arrival of self-driving cars has proved far slower and more difficult than early predictions suggested, and the question of whether and how they should be introduced has become more complicated rather than less. Some of the companies involved have scaled back their ambitions or left the field entirely, and the gap between promise and reality has itself become part of the debate.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The strongest argument for automation concerns safety. The great majority of road accidents involve human error, whether through distraction, fatigue, alcohol or poor judgement, and a machine that never tires or looks at a phone might be expected to avoid many of them. Olusegun Ade, who researches road safety, cautions that this argument is often overstated. Human drivers, he points out, cover very long distances between serious accidents, and a self-driving system must match that record across the full range of weather, roads and unexpected events before it can be said to be safer, which requires far more testing than has yet been done. He also notes that the statistics published by developers are not always comparable with official accident figures.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The technical difficulties lie less in routine driving than in rare situations. Karen Liu, a transport engineer, explains that current systems handle motorways and well-mapped streets reasonably well, but struggle with unusual events: a police officer directing traffic by hand, a child running out from behind a parked van, road works that change the layout overnight. Because such events are individually rare but collectively common, a system can perform well for thousands of hours and then fail in a way that a human driver would not. Bad weather adds a further difficulty, since rain, snow and fog can confuse the sensors on which the systems depend. Engineers can test systems in computer simulations, but a simulation includes only the situations its designers imagined.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Partial automation raises its own risks. Many new cars can steer, brake and keep their distance on motorways, while requiring the driver to remain ready to take over. Liu notes that people are poor at monitoring a system that works well most of the time; their attention drifts, and when the system suddenly hands back control, they may need several seconds to understand the situation. She regards this intermediate stage as potentially more dangerous than either full human control or full automation. Some manufacturers use cameras to check that drivers are watching the road.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The effects on cities may be larger than the effects on safety. Marta Novak, an urban planner, argues that if self-driving cars are owned privately and used as a more comfortable way of commuting, they could increase traffic, since people may be willing to travel further and empty cars may drive around rather than park. If instead they are shared and integrated with public transport, they could reduce the number of vehicles and free large areas of land now used for parking. Which outcome occurs, she says, depends on policy rather than technology. Some cities have already begun to reduce parking requirements in anticipation of such changes, and freight companies are particularly interested, since drivers account for a large share of their costs.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Responsibility is another unresolved question. When a human driver causes an accident, the law generally holds the driver responsible; when a car drives itself, it is less clear whether blame should fall on the owner, the manufacturer or the developer of the software. James Whitfield, a legal scholar, argues that manufacturers should be held responsible for accidents that occur while their systems are in control, since only they can understand and improve the technology. Several countries have begun to adopt this approach, but international agreement is still lacking. Insurance companies are also adjusting their policies, though practice varies widely.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Public attitudes are mixed. Surveys in several countries have found that many people are uneasy about travelling in a car without a driver, and that confidence falls sharply after widely reported accidents involving test vehicles, even when such accidents are far rarer than those caused by human drivers. Ade suggests that people judge machines more harshly than they judge each other, and that a self-driving system may need to be much safer than human drivers before it is accepted. Trust also appears to grow with experience, as people who have ridden in such vehicles tend to be more positive.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The most realistic prospect is a gradual and uneven introduction. Self-driving vehicles are likely to appear first in limited settings, such as goods vehicles on motorways, shuttles on fixed routes and taxis in selected cities with good weather and detailed maps, before spreading more widely. Whether they ultimately make roads safer and cities better will depend not only on the technology but on decisions about ownership, regulation and responsibility that have hardly begun to be made. Rural areas, with poorly marked roads, are likely to be among the last to see them.
paragraphs.label: H
